hints: Think of Ka as products over reactants for the acid dissociation, remembering that water as a pure liquid is omitted from the expression.
walkthrough:
Picture what Ka measures**
You have $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{HPO}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_3\text{O}^+$. $K_a$ tells you how far this proton donation goes. Like any equilibrium constant, put the concentrations of the products on top and the acid on the bottom.

Leave out water**
Water is present in huge excess as the solvent, so its concentration is effectively constant and is built into the $K_a$ value. That leaves only $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ and $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ on top and $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ below, giving $K_a = \frac{[\text{HPO}_4^{2-}][\text{H}_3\text{O}^+]}{[\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-]}$.

hints: Focus on the key property of a buffer, what happens to pH when you try to change it.
Remember the condition is for small additions, and it must work for both acid and base.
walkthrough:
Think of a shock absorber for pH**
In cells, enzymes only work if pH stays almost constant. A buffer does not keep pH fixed forever, it resists change. Add a little $\text{H}^+$ or $\text{OH}^-$ and the pH barely moves.

Make the definition complete**
You need both halves for full credit. It resists pH change, and it does so when small amounts of acid and base (or alkali) are added. Large amounts will overwhelm it.
Final answer: A solution that resists changes in pH when small amounts of acid or base are added.

hints: Identify the two species present in large amounts, the weak acid $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ and its conjugate base $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$, and match each to added $\text{OH}^-$ or $\text{H}^+$.
Write each removal as a simple ionic equation forming a weak acid or water, so $\text{H}^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$ do not stay free in solution.
walkthrough:
See the reservoir of both partners**
This buffer holds plenty of $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ (the acid) and $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ (the base). Added $\text{H}^+$ will be mopped up by the base, added $\text{OH}^-$ will be mopped up by the acid. That keeps free $[\text{H}^+]$ almost unchanged.

Remove added acid**
When $\text{H}^+$ enters, $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ acts as a base: $$\text{H}^+ + \text{HPO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$$ The strong acid is converted into weak acid, so $[\text{H}^+]$ stays low.

Remove added base**
When $\text{OH}^-$ enters, $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ donates a proton: $$\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{HPO}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ The strong base is neutralised to water plus the conjugate base, so pH barely rises.

Final answer: Addition of acid: $\text{H}^+ + \text{HPO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$
Addition of base: $\text{OH}^- + \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{HPO}_4^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$

hints: Convert pH 7.40 to $[\text{H}^+]$ using $[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}}$ and keep the unrounded value for the next step.
Rearrange the Ka expression to make the required ratio the subject: $[\text{HPO}_4^{2-}]/[\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-] = K_a/[\text{H}^+]$.
Substitute $K_a = 6.31 \times 10^{-8} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$ and your $[\text{H}^+]$ value, then divide to get the ratio with no units.
walkthrough:
Turn pH into hydrogen ion concentration**
Remember $\text{pH} = -\log[\text{H}^+]$, so reverse it: $$[\text{H}^+] = 10^{-\text{pH}} = 10^{-7.40}$$ On your calculator this gives $[\text{H}^+] = 3.98 \times 10^{-8} \text{ mol dm}^{-3}$. Keep extra figures until the end.

Rearrange Ka for the ratio you need**
Start from $K_a = \frac{[\text{HPO}_4^{2-}][\text{H}^+]}{[\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-]}$. Divide both sides by $[\text{H}^+]$ to isolate the base to acid ratio: $$\frac{[\text{HPO}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-]} = \frac{K_a}{[\text{H}^+]}$$ This is the Henderson-Hasselbalch idea without logs.

Substitute and calculate**
Put in the numbers: $$\frac{[\text{HPO}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-]} = \frac{6.31 \times 10^{-8}}{3.98 \times 10^{-8}} = 1.59$$ The units cancel, so the ratio has no units. A value near 1.6 means slightly more $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ than $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ is needed at pH 7.40, which makes sense because pH is slightly above $\text{p}K_a$.

hints: Think beyond normal buffering, if excess strong acid is added the $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ itself is protonated to the fully protonated acid.
walkthrough:
See what happens when buffer is overwhelmed**
Normally $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ removes $\text{H}^+$. If so much $\text{HCl}$ is added that all $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ is used up, the extra $\text{H}^+$ then protonates $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ itself.

Write the equation**
The product is phosphoric acid: $$\text{H}^+ + \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4$$ With $\text{HCl}$ shown fully: $\text{HCl} + \text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^- \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_4 + \text{Cl}^-$.

hints: Think beyond normal buffering, if excess strong base is added the $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ is deprotonated further to $\text{PO}_4^{3-}$ with water formed.
walkthrough:
See the other limit of buffering**
Normally $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ removes $\text{OH}^-$. If so much $\text{NaOH}$ is added that all $\text{H}_2\text{PO}_4^-$ is consumed, extra $\text{OH}^-$ removes a proton from $\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ itself.

Write the equation**
$\text{HPO}_4^{2-}$ acts as the acid to give phosphate: $$\text{OH}^- + \text{HPO}_4^{2-} \rightarrow \text{PO}_4^{3-} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$ This is why pH then changes sharply, the buffer capacity has been exceeded.
